assessment:
They read your commander and relax. Three mana, a 2/2, and an ability that wants one of every colour with no generic to hide in — most tables file that under "never happening" and go back to watching the ramp seat. Let them file it. You are going to make them unfile it in a hurry.

Count colours, not legends. She is 2/2 plus one for each colour among your OTHER legendary permanents, and she fetches anything cheaper than her power — so the only number you carry in your head is colours on board. One colour is ten legal cards. Two is twenty-three. Three is twenty-eight, four is all thirty-three, and five is nothing new at all. Play toward the SECOND colour like it is the game, because it is the thirteen-card jump and it is where Najeela first becomes legal. Then stop climbing at four and spend the wishes instead.

Budget one activation per turn cycle and pick the fetch accordingly. Mean available mana is 4.894 on turn five and 5.869 on turn six against a bill of five coloured pips, so build the turn around one wish and treat a second as a gift. Whether a legend you fetched this turn can help pay for another activation the same turn has not cleared a checker here — never build a turn on it.

Name the trap now, because it is the most tempting card in the deck. Jegantha is the only thing in the 99 that adds all five pips off one tap, and she costs five, so Sisay only reaches her at power six — four colours already on board. The fix arrives after you stopped needing it. Fetch your mana early on the ladder or draw it, and treat Jegantha as a reward rather than a repair.

One entry follows, because there is no second searcher anywhere in the 99. Twenty-six cards are non-legendary and outside her at any power — every counterspell, both free protection instants, three of the six things that can pay her bill. Fetch only what she alone can reach. Draw the rest, and stop wishing for cards she was never going to find.

targets.scenario: THE DEFAULT. Turn five, four-player pod, nobody has committed anything frightening. Sisay landed on turn three — the median across ten thousand goldfish runs — and Yoshimaru is the only other legend you control, so she is a 3/3 and the gate reads "cheaper than three." You have four lands and Birds of Paradise untapped, and between them they cover all five colours. That is exactly one activation and no more.
targets.why: Buy the knee with your first wish. At one colour you are picking from ten cards; Kinnan is a two-drop carrying two colours you do not have, so he takes you to three colours and twenty-eight legal targets off a single activation. Nothing else you can reach today moves the number that far. He also pays the bill you actually struggle with — tap Birds of Paradise or Bloom Tender and he hands you another mana of what it produced, and your activation is five coloured pips with zero generic. So take the gold two-drop over the flashy three-drop every time you are sitting on one colour. Mean available mana on turn five is 4.894, which means five sources on turn five puts you slightly ahead of the curve: spend it, do not admire it.

citations.quote: know your number — the count of bodies, spells, or mana at which the deck actually goes over the top

targets.scenario: THE BEHIND FETCH. The sweeper resolved on turn six and took the whole board. You re-cast Sisay last turn at two more than she cost the first time, she survived the round, and she is alone — a 2/2, gate reading "cheaper than two," which is three cards in the entire deck. It is turn eight, you untap with seven sources, and your hand is lands. The player who cast the sweeper is rebuilding with a rock and a three-drop.
targets.why: Take the rung, not the rock. Mox Amber is legal here too and it adds no colour at all, so it leaves the gate exactly where the sweeper left it — and the third legal card is Mikaeus, who is put onto the battlefield rather than cast, which is an open question here and not a plan. Yoshimaru is white, and that is the whole point: he makes her a 3/3 tonight and opens ten targets on your next untap, and he takes a counter every time a legend lands after him. One one-drop is not overextending, so fire the activation instead of sandbagging it. Then take the wide fetch next turn and keep your best legend in hand for their second sweeper.

citations.quote: After the wrath, initiative goes to whoever rebuilds cheapest: redeploy worst-first, keeping the best threat in hand for their second sweeper.

targets.scenario: THE CLOSING FETCH. Turn seven, second main phase. Derevi has been out since last turn and connected this combat, so three colours make Sisay a 5/5 and the gate reads "cheaper than five." You held five sources back through combat and they cover all five colours. You control four other creatures beside Derevi; the seat to your right is tapped out and the other two have two mana up between them.
targets.why: Fetch her AFTER combat, not before — she cannot attack the turn she arrives, so a pre-combat fetch buys you nothing but a turn of warning. Take her with the mana you deliberately did not spend, hold your protection for her rather than for Sisay, and untap into the checked script. Stack 002 is that script and it assumes exactly this board: she and Derevi both out since before your turn. Combat one is funded by the five sources you untap with, combat two breaks even at five untap triggers against a five-mana cost, combat three runs a surplus, the first opponent dies during combat four and the second by combat six — at zero life paid, because Command Tower plus Plaza of Heroes cover all five colours and City of Brass never has to be tapped. What the loop needs is not card count: it is five creatures connecting and five colours available every single combat. Count the table's open mana before you announce the fetch, because this is the wish that makes you the archenemy.

citations.quote: assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, and count the table's open mana before committing

A creature’s activated ability with the tap symbol or the untap symbol in its activation cost can’t be activated unless the creature has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began. A creature can’t attack unless it has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began.

targets.scenario: THE ONE NOBODY SEES COMING. Two colours among your other legends, so Sisay is a 4/4 and the gate reads "cheaper than four" — twenty-three cards. The combo seat has been drawing three a turn, just passed with four mana up and two cards in hand, and every counterspell you own is somewhere in the library where you cannot go and get it.
targets.why: Fetch a planeswalker off a permanent tutor and watch three people recalculate what your commander does. Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery — that is the held counterspell gone, the instant-speed removal aimed at your colour rungs gone, and the combo seat's end step turned off. He is legal from the second colour onward, and he is the nearest thing to tutorable interaction you own, because every counterspell in this deck is non-legendary and permanently outside her reach. So take him the turn BEFORE the combo seat needs answering; a held answer you never got to hold is worth nothing. Keep the minus-three in your pocket for a permanent already on the battlefield.

citations.quote: held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now

tutors.notes: Never activate into a cold board. At power two the gate is "cheaper than two" and there are no legendary lands in the deck to make that pool comfortable — land a colour-diverse legend first and fire on the next untap instead. Know your second choice before you announce the first: a table that answers a colour rung in response can leave you choosing from a shorter list than you planned, and that interaction has not cleared a checker here, so play around it rather than through it. And remember that the colours she gains power from are not colours you can spend — Najeela on the battlefield is one red permanent, and Esika arrives green side up, so neither of them fixes the black source you are short of. When the board is fine and it is the MANA that is stuck, the wish is Selvala: at Sisay 5/5 one tap is five mana in any combination, the entire bill. Her ability taps, so go and get her the turn before you need her, not the turn you do.

gaps:
One tutor, one wish list. There is no second searcher in the 99, so nothing here is redundant and every activation you waste is one you do not get back — which is the argument for one deliberate wish per turn cycle rather than two hopeful ones. The blind spot is structural, so build your turns around it instead of resenting it: twenty-six cards are non-legendary and unreachable at any power, including every counterspell, both free protection instants, all four Game Changers and three of the six things that can pay her five pips. She finds payoffs; you draw fuel and stack-speed protection. That makes your mulligan an enabler decision rather than a payoff decision — keep the hand with the mana, and trust the 79.8% of games in which the sim has protection available by turn six.

Two questions sit underneath this list and neither has cleared a checker here: whether a legend fetched this turn can help pay for a second activation the same turn, and what a Mikaeus put onto the battlefield arrives as. Plan on one wish per turn cycle and let the extra one be a bonus when the game hands it to you. And do not count the Bridge as a second tutor — fetch Esika and you get the green side, which is a face that ramps rather than a face that searches.
